title: A bundle still has loose ends
hook: Three cords tied in the middle, or with their ends tucked. Which tangles less in a drawer?

knows: Everyday objects have sizes, positions and amounts
doesNotKnow: that tangles start at loose ends weaving through loops, so securing the ends matters more than tying the middle

misconception: Tying a bundle of cords in the middle stops them tangling.
objective: A tie round the middle holds the cords together, but every end stays free. A tangle starts when a free end weaves through a loop, so tucking the ends away takes away that start. The drawing counts loose ends; it does not simulate tangling.

claims.text: A tie round the middle holds the cords together, but every end stays free. A tangle starts when a free end weaves through a loop, so tucking the ends away takes away that start. The drawing counts loose ends; it does not simulate tangling.
claims.source: W-383 (2026-10-14, demo-builder): retyped from source (Raymer & Smith 2007, p.16435, which could not be opened from this host) to derivation, as FC LH-2 asked. Argument: if both ends of a cord are held, the cord is a fixed arc and no motion of its middle can change its knot type, so a new knot needs a free end to pass through a loop. A tie around the middle leaves every end free; ties that also secure the ends leave none. On the stage this is the drawing: one middle tie and 2N orange end dots, against ties at both ends and the middle with 0 end dots, for N=2..8 (src/lib/lifehacks/home-models.ts evaluateHome, homeCordScene). Earlier history: FC LH-2 held it unverified only because its sole source was unopenable. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Derivation checked; Raymer and Smith not opened and not needed. Argument: a cord whose ends are both held (by hands, or by ties that also hold the ends) forms, with the holder, a closed loop, so moving the middle cannot change its knot type; a new knot needs a free end to pass through a loop (the classic fact that you cannot tie an overhand knot without letting go of an end). A tie around the middle restricts nothing at the ends. Stage: evaluateHome end-paths gives Accessible ends = 2 × cords before, 0 after; homeCordScene draws one middle tie and 2N end dots ("N loose ends") before, and ties at x = 50, 150, 250 with no end dots ("Ends tucked into end ties") after, for every slider value 2-8. The claim says the drawing distinguishes the two; it does, and it does not claim a tangle probability. Reset to unverified 2026-10-16 by demo-builder (r11 fix plan wave W3: new prediction line, stage and reveal; engine 2). Re-verify against the rebuilt stage.

recall.question: You put one tie around the middle of a coiled cord and leave both ends hanging. How can it still tangle with its neighbours?
options: The tie makes the cord stiffer
Its free ends can weave through loops
Nothing can tangle once the middle is tied tight
recall.why: Bundling the middle keeps the strands together but leaves the ends free, and free ends weaving through loops are the tangle path. Securing the ends removes that path in the drawing.
